title: Women who carried hadith
hook: Aisha, and later scholars like Karimah al-Marwaziyyah, who taught Bukhari's Sahih

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hadith of Jibril, and your line: islam, iman, ihsan. Did you ask your real question? Day one thousand one hundred sixty-one.

Cover me, cover me. A man has come home from a cave on a mountain, his heart pounding, and those are his words to his wife. It's the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, home from Hira, at the beginning of revelation, and the report sits near the start of Sahih al-Bukhari. Who tells it? A woman: Aisha, his wife. Inside her telling, another woman answers him. And much later, a third woman would sit with this very book and teach it. Today, the women in the chains. Women who carried hadith.
screen: `COVER ME, COVER ME.` → `A WOMAN'S VOICE.` → `ONE BOOK, THREE WOMEN.`

segments.voice: First, Aisha, the narrator. She tells of the cave, the angel, the command to read, and the Prophet coming home shaken. Her account of the beginning sits on the book's opening pages. She's also the source for reports on how he prayed at night, how he lived at home, what he said in private. Second, Khadijah, inside the story. In Aisha's telling, the Prophet tells Khadijah he fears for himself. And Khadijah answers: never, by Allah, Allah will never disgrace you. Then she says why. You keep ties with your relatives. You carry the burdens of the weak. You help the one who has nothing. You honor your guest. You stand by people in their hardships. Then she takes him to her cousin Waraqah. So the first comfort in this report comes from a woman, and the report itself comes from a woman. Third, Karimah, the teacher. Long after, a scholar named Karimah al-Marwaziyyah taught Bukhari's Sahih in Mecca. Students came to read the book with her, and wrote her into their chains: she narrated it to us. Her name went into the line by which this book was handed on. Fourth, the shape of it. One book, three women. A woman tells the story. Inside the story, a woman gives the first comfort. And a woman teaches the book that holds them both. The science this path has followed for weeks asks of every narrator: trustworthy? careful? did they really hear it? Women narrators were asked the same questions. Their names are in the chains because of the answers.
screen: `AISHA TELLS IT.` · `KHADIJAH: ALLAH WILL NEVER DISGRACE YOU.` · `KARIMAH TEACHES THE BOOK.` · `THE SAME QUESTIONS, THE SAME CHAINS.`

segments.voice: The practice: learn one woman narrator. Settle, and breathe. Three women, three parts. Aisha, who told it. Khadijah, who comforted. Karimah, who taught it. Choose one, and keep her name. Then go back to Khadijah's list, line by line. Ties with relatives. The burdens of the weak. The one who has nothing. The guest. People in hardship. Which of these has someone done for you? Which one is within your reach today? Just notice. If you pray, you can remember these women in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Women who carried hadith. From Aisha, who narrated, to Karimah al-Marwaziyyah, who taught Bukhari's Sahih: women in the chains, tested like everyone else. Today's word.

Your line: she taught the sahih. Today, do one thing from Khadijah's list for someone, and if you can, thank a woman who taught you something that lasted. Tomorrow: memorizing chains. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-one.

howItsDone: Students of hadith learn the names of women narrators and teachers, from Aisha onward, and some modern scholars have gathered their lives into studies of their own.

fork.setup: you're Khadijah. your husband comes home from the mountain trembling, afraid for himself. what do you say?
options: 'never, by Allah: Allah will never disgrace you,' and you name his good deeds.
fork.reveal: she reassures him by naming what he does: keeps ties of kin, carries the weak, helps the one with nothing, honors guests. then she takes him to Waraqah.

original.note: 'she narrated to us': how a chain names a woman who taught the report.

trapdoor: what you thought: hadith came down through men.
what it means: women narrated and taught hadith, from Aisha on, and their names sit in the chains.
what a scholar hears: one book, three women: Aisha narrates, Khadijah comforts inside the story, and Karimah al-Marwaziyyah teaches the Sahih itself.

notes: Bukhari 3 (Aisha's account of the beginning of revelation; 'cover me'; Khadijah: 'never, by Allah, Allah will never disgrace you', her list of his deeds; Waraqah): confirm number and the paraphrased list.

Karimah al-Marwaziyyah taught the Sahih in Mecca and her transmission entered the chains by which the book was handed on: stated without dates; confirm. Days 1032 and 1053 (year 3) already named her; this day uses a new angle (one book, three women).
'Women narrators were asked the same questions' summarizes how hadith critics assessed women narrators; confirm phrasing.
Original: حدثتنا (haddathatna, 'she narrated to us'); pronunciation given as had-da-THAT-na. Confirm.
howItsDone 'some modern scholars have gathered their lives' alludes to Mohammad Akram Nadwi's al-Muhaddithat; not named here.

Editor: hook no longer opens on the first pages of al-Bukhari (days 1145 and 1152 used that angle); it now opens on 'cover me, cover me', and the teach's first point was adjusted so the line isn't repeated. Practice dropped the name-per-breath device used on days 1154 and 1156.
